derived_focus.primary_focus: Develop deep conceptual understanding of material properties and build independent scientific thinking through guided observation, experimentation, reasoning and measurement in a self-paced AI learning environment.
supporting_themes: Mass, Volume and Formal Definition of Matter

recommended_micro_lessons.segmentation_logic: Observation → Property Identification → Experimental Validation → Measurement → Abstract Concept (Matter)

misconception_zones: Air is not matter because it cannot be seen
assessment_sensitivity_zones: Clear differentiation between mass and volume

micro_lessons.title: Objects and Materials – Observing the World Scientifically
learning_objectives: Understand that objects may use multiple materials

ai_delivery_flow.immersion_start: Display high-resolution image grid of common household and classroom objects. Learner taps each object to reveal material composition.
ai_delivery_flow.guided_observation: Interactive prompt: 'Select an object. Now select what it is made of.' AI records responses and provides instant correction.

concept_by_IQ.foundation: Material is the substance used to make an object. Example: Bottle → plastic or steel. Chair → wood or metal.
concept_by_IQ.standard: An object may use multiple materials based on function. Example: Pen = plastic body + metal tip + ink.
concept_by_IQ.advanced: Material selection depends on properties such as strength, flexibility, heat resistance and waterproof nature. Function determines material.

ai_delivery_flow.interactive_activity: Drag-and-drop classification task: Group 10 objects by material. Then regroup by function.
ai_delivery_flow.thinking_extension: Scenario simulation: Design a tumbler. AI asks learner to choose materials and justifies suitability.
misconception_alerts: Object is not the same as material
One object can have multiple materials
ai_delivery_flow.checkpoint_quiz: 3 auto-graded reasoning MCQs with explanation layer.
ai_delivery_flow.bridge_forward: Next: If materials differ, what properties make them different?

micro_lessons.title: Appearance and Hardness – Testing and Comparing Properties

ai_delivery_flow.immersion_start: 3D rotating models of aluminium foil, copper wire, wood, rubber. Learner toggles light source to observe shine.
ai_delivery_flow.guided_experiment: Virtual scratch test simulation. Learner selects tool and material; system shows resistance level.

concept_by_IQ.foundation: Lustrous materials shine. Hard materials resist scratching. Soft materials compress easily.
concept_by_IQ.standard: Not all shiny objects are metals. Polished plastic may appear shiny. Hardness depends on comparison.
concept_by_IQ.advanced: Hardness is relative: Rubber > sponge but < iron. Material properties are comparative, not absolute.

ai_delivery_flow.interactive_activity: Rank materials from softest to hardest using drag-scale interface.
ai_delivery_flow.thinking_extension: Design a hammer. Select material based on required hardness and durability.
ai_delivery_flow.checkpoint_quiz: Short reasoning: Why are tools made of metal instead of rubber?
ai_delivery_flow.bridge_forward: Next: Can we see through all materials?

micro_lessons.title: Transparency and Light – Understanding Visibility
learning_objectives: Classify materials as transparent, translucent or opaque

ai_delivery_flow.immersion_start: Interactive hide-and-seek simulation. Learner selects hiding material and sees visibility outcome.
ai_delivery_flow.guided_visual_experiment: Place object behind glass, butter paper and wood using virtual slider.

concept_by_IQ.foundation: Transparent → clear visibility. Opaque → cannot see through. Translucent → blurred visibility.
concept_by_IQ.standard: Material choice affects privacy and lighting. Example: Bathroom glass is translucent.
concept_by_IQ.advanced: Transparency depends on how light passes through material structure. Water can become opaque if impurities are added.

ai_delivery_flow.thinking_extension: Design a classroom window that balances light and privacy.
misconception_alerts: Opaque means dark in colour only
ai_delivery_flow.checkpoint_quiz: Explain why walls are opaque and windows are transparent.
ai_delivery_flow.bridge_forward: Next: What happens when materials mix with water?

micro_lessons.title: Solubility and Mass – Observing Change Scientifically

ai_delivery_flow.immersion_start: Virtual lab with five tumblers. Learner adds sugar, salt, sand, chalk powder and sawdust.
ai_delivery_flow.experiment_phase: AI simulates stirring and shows particle-level animation.

concept_by_IQ.foundation: Soluble materials dissolve. Insoluble materials do not.
concept_by_IQ.standard: Disappearance does not mean loss; dissolved substance is still present.
concept_by_IQ.advanced: Oxygen dissolves in water and supports aquatic life. Dissolved substances still contribute to mass.

ai_delivery_flow.mass_activity: Digital weighing balance simulation comparing sand, water and pebbles.
ai_delivery_flow.thinking_extension: Explain why sugar solution still has mass even after sugar disappears.
ai_delivery_flow.checkpoint_quiz: Why does sand settle but sugar does not?
ai_delivery_flow.bridge_forward: If materials have mass, do they occupy space?

micro_lessons.title: Volume and Matter – From Observation to Definition

ai_delivery_flow.immersion_start: Two identical tumblers shown with different water levels. Learner measures volume using slider scale.

concept_by_IQ.foundation: Volume is space occupied. Mass is amount of matter.
concept_by_IQ.standard: Units: g, kg for mass; mL, L for volume. Proper unit formatting rules enforced interactively.
concept_by_IQ.advanced: Matter is anything that has mass and occupies space. Same volume objects may have different mass (cotton vs stone). Air is matter.

ai_delivery_flow.interactive_conversion: Convert 1 m3 to litres using digital calculator module.
ai_delivery_flow.thinking_extension: Why could water not fully transfer into smaller bottle? Connect to volume.
ai_delivery_flow.checkpoint_quiz: Define matter in your own words.
ai_delivery_flow.bridge_forward: Next level: Density and states of matter.
